'''''Rhododendron calendulaceum''''', the '''flame azalea''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=RHCA4|taxon=Rhododendron calendulaceum|accessdate=21 October 2015}}</ref> is a species of ''[[Rhododendron]].'' It is a deciduous shrub that grows up to 120–450 cm tall. This species of ''Rhododendron'' is native to the [[Appalachian Mountains]] in the eastern [[United States]], ranging from southern [[Pennsylvania]] and [[Ohio]] to northern [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]]. It may be extirpated from Pennsylvania and [[Alabama]].<ref name=":1" /> It occurs naturally in mixed deciduous forests and is typically found in woodland slopes and [[Appalachian balds|mountain balds]] in the Appalachians,<ref name="ncstate" /> where it prefers dry and rocky mountain woods.<ref name=":2" /> The inflorescences of ''Rhododendron calendulaceum'' are visited by many animals such as bees, butterflies, hummingbirds and small mammals.<ref name="ncstate" /> It is a popular cultivated plant due to its bright yellow, orange or red flowers. 

== Description ==
It is a [[deciduous]] [[shrub]], 120–450 cm tall. The [[leaf|leaves]] are simple, 3–7 cm long, slightly dull green above and [[wikt:villous|villous]] below. The arrangement is generally alternate, however they appear [[Whorl (botany)|whorled]] towards the tips of the branches.

The [[flower]]s are 4–5 cm long, usually bright orange, but can vary from pastel orange to dark reddish-orange. These non-fragrant flowers have 4-5 lobes and grow in clusters of 5–10. It typically blooms in late May and early June.<ref name="ncstate">{{Cite web|title=Rhododendron calendulaceum (Flame Azalea) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox|url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/rhododendron-calendulaceum/|access-date=2020-06-10|website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=Brand|first=Mark H.|date=|title=Plant Database|url=http://www.hort.uconn.edu/plants/detail.php?pid=393|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=2020-06-10|website=www.hort.uconn.edu}}</ref>

=== Variation in wild populations ===
''Rhododendron calendulaceum'' is a highly variable species. The flowers of ''Rhododendron calendulaceum'' can range from light yellow to orange and rarely, a scarlet red. Some flowers appear to be a blend of multiple colors, and others seem to have secondary pigments such as pink or red. Some have even reported a white flower in ''Rhododendron calendulaceum'', however these records cannot be verified. The [[buds]] of ''Rhododendron calendulaceum'' are typically a darker color than the mature flower, however some flowers deepen in color with age. In some plants, a full range of colors such as yellows, oranges and reds can be present on the same plant. It is possible that color change is affected by light, with flowers in shadier areas exhibiting less color change compared to plants in open spaces.<ref name="donaldhyatt">{{Cite journal|last1=Hyatt|first1=Donald W.|last2=McLellan|first2=George Keen|title=''Rhododendron calendulaceum'': Variations in the Wild|url=http://www.donaldhyatt.com/articles/Calendulaceum-Article-Illustrated.pdf|journal=Yearbook of the Rhododendron Species Foundation Botanical Garden|access-date=19 December 2023}}</ref>

The flower sizes in ''Rhododendron calendulaceum'' are also variable, with a typical flower size of 2-2.5 inches. Some flowers have blossoms of less than an inch, while others can be up to 3 inches.<ref name="donaldhyatt"/>

== Ecology ==
The inflorescences of ''Rhododendron calendulaceum'' are visited by a diverse group of animals such as bees, butterflies, hummingbirds and small mammals.<ref name="ncstate"/> The flowers can only be pollinated by the wings of butterflies. Only ''[[Papilio glaucus]]'' and ''[[Speyeria cybele]]'' have been observed pollinating the flowers. ''P. glaucus'' is more effective in pollination due to differences in wing flapping behavior.<ref name="Reproduction in Flame Azalea">{{Cite journal |title=Reproduction in Flame Azalea (''Rhododendron calendulaceum'', Ericaceae): A Rare Case of Insect Wing Pollination |journal= The American Naturalist |date=2 August 2015 |author1=Epps, Mary Jane |author2=Allison, Suzanne E. |author3=Wolfe, Lorne M. |author4=McPeek, Mark A. |volume=186 |issue=2 |doi=10.1086/682006 |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/682006|access-date=19 December 2023|url-access=subscription }}</ref> ''Rhododendron calendulaceum'' is a host of the fungus ''[[Exobasidium vaccinii]]''. ''E. vaccinii'' negatively affects the reproduction and health of the flowers and branches of ''Rhododendron calendulaceum''.<ref>{{Cite journal |title=Reproductive consequences of a gall-inducing fungal pathogen (''Exobasidium vaccinii'') on ''Rhododendron calendulaceum'' (Ericaceae)|journal=Canadian Journal of Botany |date=January 2000 |author1=Wolfe, Lorne M. |author2=Rissler, Leslie J |volume=77 |issue=10 |doi=10.1139/b99-108 |url=https://cdnsciencepub.com/doi/abs/10.1139/b99-108?journalCode=cjb1|access-date=19 December 2023|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The insect ''[[Rhinocapsus vanduzeei]]'' is known to feed on the stamens of ''Rhododendron calendulaceum'' flowers.<ref>{{Cite journal |title=A Potential Insect Pest of Azaleas|journal=American Rhododendron Society |author1=Wheeler, A. G. |url=https://scholar.lib.vt.edu/ejournals/JARS/v33n1/v33n1-wheeler.htm|access-date=19 December 2023}}</ref> ''Rhododendron calendulaceum'' is a host plant for the larvae of ''[[Euura lipovskyi]]''.<ref>{{Cite journal |title=First record of Azalea Sawfly (''Euura lipovskyi'', Hymenoptera: Tenthredinidae) in Canada|journal=The Canadian Field-Naturalist |author1=Goulet, Henri |author2=Catling, Paul |author3=Kostiuk, Brenda |doi=10.22621/cfn.v136i1.2859
|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/362374395_First_record_of_Azalea_Sawfly_Euura_lipovskyi_Hymenoptera_Tenthredinidae_in_Canada|access-date=25 April 2024|doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Distribution and habitat==
This species of ''Rhododendron'' is native to the [[Appalachian Mountains]] in the eastern [[United States]], ranging from southern [[Pennsylvania]] and [[Ohio]] to northern [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]]. It may be extirpated from Pennsylvania and [[Alabama]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|date=2000|title=Flame Azalea|url=https://vnps.org/wp-content/uploads/dlm_uploads/2020/06/2000-Flame-Azalea-Rhododendron-calendulaceum-WOY-Brochure.pdf|access-date=21 December 2023|publisher=Virginia Native Plant Society|website=vnps.org}}</ref> The state of Pennsylvania lists ''Rhododendron calendulaceum'' as extirpated from the state.<ref>{{Cite web|title=CHAPTER 45. CONSERVATION OF PENNSYLVANIA NATIVE WILD PLANTS|url=https://www.pacodeandbulletin.gov/Display/pacode?file=/secure/pacode/data/017/chapter45/chap45toc.html&d=|access-date=21 December 2023|publisher=COMMONWEALTH OF PENNSYLVANIA|website=www.pacodeandbulletin.gov}}</ref> It has been reported historically in [[New York (state)|New York]] and [[Maryland]], however, its current native status in these states is undetermined.<ref> {{Cite web|last=Carey|first=Jennifer H.|date=1994|title=Rhododendron calendulaceum|url=https://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/shrub/rhocae/all.html|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=2020-06-10|website=www.fs.fed.us}} </ref> However, it can occur as an [[introduced species]] in anthropogenic habitats. It occurs naturally in mixed deciduous forests. It is typically found in woodland slopes and [[Appalachian balds|mountain balds]] in the Appalachians,<ref name="ncstate"/> where it prefers dry and rocky mountain woods.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|title=''Rhododendron calendulaceum''|url=https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=rhca4|access-date=10 December 2023|website=www.wildflower.org}}</ref> It lives in a variety of forest ecosystems such as Loblolly-shortleaf pine, [[Oak–hickory forest|oak-hickory]] and [[Beech–maple forest|maple-beech-birch forests]]. It prefers to be covered by ''[[Quercus montana]]'', ''[[Quercus alba]]'', ''[[Quercus velutina]]'' and ''[[Quercus rubra]]''. ''Rhododendron calendulaceum'' primarily occurs in mixed deciduous forests. It is found in the well-developed shrub layer of [[Quercus|oaks]] with southern and western sun exposure. It is commonly found in ravines with mesic soil. ''Rhododendron calendulaceum'' is an important understory shrub in forests that were formerly co-dominated by the [[American chestnut]]. ''Rhododendron calendulaceum'' commonly occurs with other ericaceous shrubs including ''[[Rhododendron maximum]]'', ''[[Kalmia latifolia]]'', ''[[Vaccinium corymbosum]]'', and [[Gaylussacia|''Gaylussacia'' spp.]] ''Rhododendron calendulaceum'' commonly occurs in oak forest that periodically see fire.<ref name="USDA">{{Cite web|title=SPECIES: ''Rhododendron calendulaceum''|url=https://www.fs.usda.gov/database/feis/plants/shrub/rhocae/all.html#30|access-date=20 December 2023|publisher=Fire Effects Information System |website=www.fs.usda.gov}}</ref> ''Rhododendron calendulaceum'' grows in well-drained, mesic to moist, medium to fine textured soils in part shade. ''Rhododendron calendulaceum'' prefers a pH range of 4.3 to 5.8. ''Rhododendron calendulaceum'' requires a minimum soil depth of 14 in. ''Rhododendron calendulaceum'' requires at least a 200 day growing season.<ref>{{cite book |last=Mehl |first=Geoffrey |date=2016 |title=Pennsylvania Naturally |publisher=Pennystone Books |page=352 |isbn=9780986276606 }}</ref>
[[File:Rhododendron_calendulaceum_in_Lumpkin_county,_GA.jpg|200px|thumb|right|''Rhododendron calendulaceum'' in the shrub layer under oaks]]

== Horticulture ==
The flame azalea is a popular [[Horticulture|cultivated plant]], primarily due to its showy flowers. Many [[Cultivar|cultivars]] and domestic varieties exist, including Chattooga, Cherokee, Golden Sunset Flame, Golden Yellow Flame, Smokey Mountaineer and Wahsega.<ref name=":0" /> It is also an important parent species in hybrid Azaleas, such as Ghent, Knap Hill, Maid in the Shade, Mollis and Northern Lights.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Deciduous Azaleas|url=http://www.rhodyman.net/rhodyde.html|access-date=2020-06-10|website=www.rhodyman.net}}</ref>
